t: Replace the Substring for Balanced String — Sliding Window Editorial
o: We must pick one contiguous substring and replace it with any characters so that, afterwards, every character appears exactly n/4 times. Equivalently, the part of the string *outside* the replaced window must not contain more than n/4 copies of any character — the window can then be filled to fix all deficits. Checking the examples: "QWER" needs nothing (0); in "QQWE" a single 'Q' is over quota (2 > 1), so replacing that one character suffices; in "QQQW" two excess 'Q's force a window of length 2. Since n can be 10^5, an O(n^2) enumeration of windows is too slow; we need a linear scan. The key structural fact is monotonicity: if a window of some length works, any longer window containing it also works, which invites a sliding-window / two-pointer solution.
k: A window is valid iff every character outside it occurs at most n/4 times; then the window itself can always be rewritten to balance the string.
Validity is monotone in window size: extending a valid window keeps it valid, so two pointers find the minimum in O(n).
If the string is already balanced, the answer is 0 — handle this before/within the loop.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute Force with Prefix Counts
a.i: For every pair (i, j), count occurrences of each character inside s[i..j] using prefix sums, and check whether the outside counts are all ≤ n/4. This directly implements the validity condition but costs O(n^2) time, which is too slow for n = 10^5; it is included mainly to build intuition for the sliding window.
s: Count total frequency of each of Q, W, E, R; target = n/4.
Build prefix count arrays for each character.
For each left index i, for each right index j ≥ i, compute outside counts as total minus inside counts.
If all outside counts ≤ target, record j - i + 1 as a candidate answer.
Return the minimum candidate (0 if already balanced).
a.t: O(n^2) — O(n^2) window pairs, each checked in O(1) via prefix counts. Too slow for n = 10^5.
a.sp: O(n) — four prefix-count arrays of length n+1.

a.i: Maintain a running count of characters inside the current window [l, r]. A window is valid when, after removing its contents, no character exceeds n/4 outside. Because extending a valid window never invalidates it, we can advance r while shrinking l greedily whenever the window becomes valid, guaranteeing minimal lengths are seen. Each pointer moves at most n times, giving linear time.
s: Count total frequency of each character; set target = n/4.
For each right index, add s[right] to the window count.
While the window is valid (total[c] minus window[c] ≤ target for all c), update answer with right - left + 1 and remove s[left], incrementing left.

c.python:
class Solution:
    def balancedString(self, s: str) -> int:
        n = len(s)
        target = n // 4
        cnt = Counter(s)
        win = defaultdict(int)
        need = lambda: all(cnt[c] - win[c] <= target for c in 'QWER')
        ans = n
        left = 0
        for right, ch in enumerate(s):
            win[ch] += 1
            while need():
                ans = min(ans, right - left + 1)
                win[s[left]] -= 1
                left += 1
        return ans

a.t: O(n) — both pointers traverse the string once; each validity check is O(4) = O(1).
a.sp: O(1) — fixed-size arrays of length 4 for counts.

w: In an interview, go straight to the sliding window after stating the key reformulation (outside counts ≤ n/4); mention brute force only briefly to justify why O(n^2) fails. Common pitfalls: forgetting to handle the already-balanced case (the loop naturally returns 0 since the empty window is valid — verify your shrink condition allows this); checking whether the *window* rather than the *outside* satisfies quotas; and off-by-one errors on window length (right − left + 1). Edge cases: perfectly balanced input (answer 0), all four characters identical except forced imbalance (e.g., "QQQQ" → answer 3), and n = 4. Follow-ups might ask to output the actual replacement substring (any fill achieving exact quotas works — greedily assign deficit characters), or to generalize to k distinct characters with quota n/k, where the same technique applies unchanged.
